title: Key management and storing secrets
summary: Rotation with versioned keys, what a KMS, HSM and Key Vault really do, ASP.NET Core Data Protection, and where secrets must never live.

steps.title: A key has a lifecycle
body: Every key goes through the same stages: **generate** (from a CSPRNG, ideally inside the HSM), **store** (somewhere access-controlled and audited), **use**, **rotate** (a new version takes over encryption), **retire** (old version only decrypts), and **destroy** (once no data needs it).
The services that do this for you:
- An **HSM** (hardware security module) is tamper-resistant hardware that generates and uses keys without ever exporting them. You send it data; it sends back results.
- A **KMS** (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS) and **Azure Key Vault** are cloud services built on HSMs. They add access policies, automatic rotation, and an audit log of every use of every key.
- Your app authenticates to them with a **managed identity** or workload identity, so there is no password to leak in the first place.

steps.prompt: Match each term to what it is.
pairs: Tamper-resistant hardware that uses keys without exporting them
A cloud service that holds keys, enforces access policy and logs every use
A label stored with ciphertext saying which key to decrypt with
How an app proves who it is to the vault without a stored password
Destroying data by deleting the only key that can decrypt it
steps.explain: In practice you rarely hold a master key in your process at all: you hold permission to ask the vault to use it.

steps.title: Versioned keys make rotation safe
body: Rotation must not break data encrypted yesterday. The standard trick: **prefix every ciphertext with the id of the key that made it**.
```text
v1:Zr8y...    <- written last year, still readable
v2:Q0bT...    <- written today with the current key

Encrypt always uses the **current** key. Decrypt reads the prefix and looks the key up. Rotating is then just "add v3 and make it current". Old values are re-encrypted lazily (on next write) or by a background job, and v1 is retired only when no value uses it. JWTs do the same with the `kid` header (see the *Authentication & JWT* topic's JWKS lesson).

steps.prompt: Before retiring v1, you count which key each stored value uses. What does this print?
steps.explain: Two values still need v1, so v1 cannot be destroyed yet. The key id in front of every value is what makes this question answerable at all.

steps.title: A key ring
prompt: Write two methods over a key ring `Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys` (key id to 32-byte AES key):
- `string Encrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string currentId, byte[] nonce, string text)` returns `"<currentId>:<Base64 of nonce + ciphertext + tag>"` using AES-GCM.

- `string Decrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string token)` reads the id before the **first** `:`, looks the key up, and decrypts. An unknown id throws `KeyNotFoundException` (the dictionary indexer does that for you).
The tests encrypt with `v1`, rotate to `v2`, and check both still decrypt.
starter: string Encrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string currentId, byte[] nonce, string text)
string Decrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string token)
solution: string Encrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string currentId, byte[] nonce, string text)
gcm.Encrypt(nonce, plain, box.AsSpan(12, plain.Length), box.AsSpan(12 + plain.Length));
string Decrypt(Dictionary<string, byte[]> keys, string token)
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoKeys = new Dictionary<string, byte[]> { ["v1"] = Enumerable.Repeat((byte)1, 32).ToArray() };
var dojoN1 = new byte[12]; dojoN1[11] = 1;
var dojoN2 = new byte[12]; dojoN2[11] = 2;
var dojoOld = Encrypt(dojoKeys, "v1", dojoN1, "written last year");
Dojo.Check("the token starts with its key id", dojoOld.StartsWith("v1:"), dojoOld);
dojoKeys["v2"] = Enumerable.Repeat((byte)2, 32).ToArray();
var dojoNew = Encrypt(dojoKeys, "v2", dojoN2, "written today");
Dojo.Check("new tokens use the current key", dojoNew.StartsWith("v2:"), dojoNew);
Dojo.Eq("old values still decrypt after rotation", "written last year", Decrypt(dojoKeys, dojoOld));
Dojo.Eq("new values decrypt", "written today", Decrypt(dojoKeys, dojoNew));
Dojo.Throws<KeyNotFoundException>("an unknown key id is refused", () => Decrypt(dojoKeys, "v9:" + dojoNew[3..]));
Dojo.Throws<System.Security.Cryptography.AuthenticationTagMismatchException>("relabelling a v2 value as v1 fails", () => Decrypt(dojoKeys, "v1:" + dojoNew[3..]));
hints: `token.IndexOf(':')` finds the split; `token[..colon]` is the id and `token[(colon + 1)..]` the Base64.
Base64 never contains `:`, so splitting at the first colon is safe.

steps.title: ASP.NET Core Data Protection
body: For the common web jobs (auth cookies, antiforgery tokens, short-lived protected payloads) ASP.NET Core ships the **Data Protection** system, and you should use it instead of hand-rolled AES:
```csharp
var protector = provider.CreateProtector("Orders.ShareLinks.v1");   // a purpose string
string token = protector.Protect("order:42");
string back  = protector.Unprotect(token);                          // throws if tampered

It manages a **key ring** for you: keys rotate every 90 days by default, every payload carries the id of the key that protected it (exactly the versioning you just built), and old keys keep decrypting. Different purpose strings get independent derived keys. Two things you must configure in production: **persist the key ring** to shared storage (a blob container, a database, a mounted volume) and **protect it at rest** (`ProtectKeysWithAzureKeyVault`, a certificate, or DPAPI on Windows).
It needs the ASP.NET Core framework, so it is not runnable in this topic's exercises.

steps.prompt: An app runs on three instances behind a load balancer. Users are logged out at random whenever a request lands on a different instance. The most likely cause?
options: Each instance generated its own Data Protection key ring, so cookies from one cannot be unprotected by another
TLS is terminated at the load balancer
steps.explain: Without a shared, persisted key ring each instance invents its own keys (and loses them on restart). Persist the ring to shared storage and protect it with a vault key.

steps.title: Secrets do not belong in code
body: A key in source code is in every clone, every build agent, every container image and **the git history forever**, even after you delete the line. Treat any secret that reached a repository as leaked: rotate it, then clean up.
Where secrets live instead:
| Environment | Store |
| your machine | `dotnet user-secrets`, a local `.env` that is git-ignored |
| CI | the pipeline's secret store, injected as environment variables |
| production | a vault (Key Vault, Secrets Manager), read with a managed identity; or environment variables set by the platform |

Load secrets at startup, **fail closed** when one is missing (never fall back to a built-in "dev" key), and never log them. The *Authentication & JWT* topic's **Secrets and logging** lesson covers scanning, redaction and logging in depth.

steps.prompt: Is each place acceptable for a production encryption key?
items: A cloud key vault, read with a managed identity
An environment variable set by the hosting platform
A `const string` in the source code
An HSM that never exports it
steps.explain: Anything that ends up in the repository or the image is readable by everyone who can read those.

steps.title: Load the key, fail closed
prompt: This loader falls back to a built-in key when the environment variable is missing, so a misconfigured production server silently encrypts everything with a key that is in the source code.
Fix `byte[] LoadKey(Func<string, string?> getEnv)` (the tests pass a fake environment):
- if it is missing or empty, throw `InvalidOperationException`;
- if it does not decode to exactly 32 bytes, throw `InvalidOperationException` too. Never include the value in the message.
solution: throw new InvalidOperationException("VAULT_KEY is not set.");
throw new InvalidOperationException($"VAULT_KEY must decode to 32 bytes, got {key.Length}.");
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoGood = Convert.ToBase64String(Enumerable.Range(0, 32).Select(i => (byte)i).ToArray());
Dojo.Eq("a 32-byte key loads", Enumerable.Range(0, 32).Select(i => (byte)i).ToArray(), LoadKey(n => n == "VAULT_KEY" ? dojoGood : null));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("a missing key fails closed", () => LoadKey(_ => null));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("an empty key fails closed", () => LoadKey(_ => ""));
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("a 16-byte key is refused", () => LoadKey(_ => "AwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAw=="));
Dojo.Try("the error never contains the value", () =>
try { LoadKey(_ => "AwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAwMDAw=="); }
catch (InvalidOperationException e) { Dojo.Check("the message does not echo the key", !e.Message.Contains("AwMD"), e.Message); }
hints: Delete the fallback line entirely: there is no safe default key.
